column4: From a sperm-drop God “created him, then measured him” (خَلَقَهُۥ فَقَدَّرَهُۥ), reproducing the section’s creation-as-prior-measure in one human-making act.
After 80:19’s creation and measuring, God makes the path easy (ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُۥ); the sequence joins measured making, direction, and ease exactly as this section joins 87:2, 87:3, and 87:8.
Moses defines “our Lord” as the one who gave every thing its created form and then guided it; this is the closest full parallel to the craftsman-like sequence “created/proportioned, measured/guided.”
God created every thing and determined it with exact determination (فَقَدَّرَهُۥ تَقْدِيرًا), making measure intrinsic to creation rather than a later lottery of shares.
“We created every thing by measure” (خَلَقْنَٰهُ بِقَدَرٍ) states directly the section’s claim that each made thing has an assigned measure.
Abraham says that the one who created him is the one who guides him; his wording unites the two acts and also answers the surah’s final naming of Abraham’s scrolls.
The human is addressed by the Lord “who created you, proportioned you, and balanced you”; the sequence turns creation into the fitting and straightening of a made body.
From the clot God “created and proportioned” (فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ), repeating 87:2 within the staged making of a human.
After the drop is lodged until a known measure in 77:20–22, “We measured, and excellent are We at measuring” makes divine determination the governing act of the whole gestational scene.
The sequence begins by creating the human from lowly water; 77:21–23 then show the placement, known limit, and measuring that complete this cited row’s act of creation.
God places the drop in a secure resting place, giving the section’s abstract preparation a concrete fitted receptacle; 77:22 supplies its limit and 77:23 its measuring.
The embryo remains “until a known measure” (إِلَىٰ قَدَرٍ مَّعْلُومٍ), displaying both the assigned amount and the terminal point named in the section’s dictionary sense.
God knows what every womb bears, what it diminishes and increases, and “every thing with Him is by a measure”; the womb makes hidden variation part of exact apportionment.
God measures the earth’s provisions in four days, “equal for those who ask”; قَدَّرَ and سَوَآءً meet in an act that fits and apportions sustenance.
Every thing’s treasuries are with God, and He sends it down only in a known measure; this distinguishes the true giver’s measured allotment from a share won by chance.
“God has made for every thing a measure” (قَدْ جَعَلَ ٱللَّهُ لِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ قَدْرًا) is the section’s “every thing has an amount and term” stated as a universal rule.
David is commanded to make ample coats of mail and “measure precisely in the links” (وَقَدِّرْ فِى ٱلسَّرْدِ); it is a literal workshop scene of planning, fitting, and finishing parts.
Paradisal silver vessels are “measured with exact measure” (قَدَّرُوهَا تَقْدِيرًا), a finished container whose capacity is fitted as precisely as the section’s cut hide vessel.
The sun runs toward its appointed resting point, “the measuring of the Mighty, the Knowing”; measure here includes both directed motion and a destination, like the fitted arrow’s point.
God measures the moon through stations until it returns like an old date stalk; the verse makes measure a course with a visible end and also lets a made form age into thinness.
The sun and moon are made for reckoning, and this is called the precise determination of the Mighty, the Knowing; cosmic regularity displays measure as calculated order.
God measures the moon into stations so people can know years and calculation; measured stages give a created light a course and an intelligible end.
God sends water down from heaven “in measure” and settles it in the earth; measured liquid and a prepared repository echo the section’s making of a vessel to hold water.
Water descends from heaven by measure and revives a dead land; its allotted quantity is directed to a life-giving end rather than assigned by chance.
God measures night and day, knows people cannot calculate them fully, and permits whatever recitation is easy (مَا تَيَسَّرَ); divine measuring and granted ease meet in one ayah.
“We have apportioned death among you” makes determination an inescapable distributed limit, directly illustrating the dictionary claim that every thing has a measure and a term.
The earth brings forth “every thing measured” (مِن كُلِّ شَىْءٍ مَّوْزُونٍ); living provision itself appears fitted to weight and proportion.
God raised the heaven’s structure and proportioned it (فَسَوَّىٰهَا), presenting تسوية as the finishing of a vast constructed form.
The moving mountains are called “the workmanship of God, who perfected every thing”; explicit craft language supports the section’s hearing creation as skilled fabrication.
God “made excellent the creation of every thing” and begins human creation from clay, stressing the fitted quality of the created product.
The seven layered heavens show no disparity in the Merciful’s creation; the invitation to inspect them for a fissure makes sound proportion visibly testable.
“The Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner” presents divine making through distinct craft-like names, followed by the glorification that 87:1 commands.
God forms people in the womb however He wills; hidden bodily formation supplies the concrete workshop implied by measuring before shaping.
God creates people in their mothers’ wombs “creation after creation” through three darknesses, enacting the section’s definition of lordly nurture as stage-by-stage formation.
“You were created in stages” (خَلَقَكُمْ أَطْوَارًا) condenses the section’s account of bringing a thing through successive states toward completion.
The embryo passes through several fashioned states and becomes another creation; “best of creators” marks the completed result of the staged craft.
Creation from dust and then a drop, hidden pregnancy, and every lengthened or shortened life written in a book join bodily making to its measured span.
The long sequence from dust and drop through womb, birth, maturity, death, and decrepitude displays creation as preparation through successive states to differing limits.
God brings people from dust and a drop through childhood to maturity and an appointed term, making both stepwise nurture and its endpoint explicit.
Humanity is created “in the finest proportion” (فِىٓ أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ), a bodily counterpart to the section’s smooth, straight, correctly fitted product.
God makes dwellings from cattle hides that are light in travel and settlement; this is the Quran’s clearest scene of hide deliberately turned into a useful constructed object.
Wine, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are declared defilement, then “avoid it so that you may prosper” joins the very lot scene to 87’s roots for avoidance and flourishing.
Wine and gambling have benefits but their sin is greater than their benefit; the judgment directly tests the section’s water-skin term nifʿ against the apparent gain of maysir.
Seeking allotted shares by divining arrows (تَسْتَقْسِمُوا۟ بِٱلْأَزْلَٰمِ) is forbidden, directly staging the section’s arrow-based search for a portion.
This ayah explains 5:90’s ban: gambling creates enmity and blocks remembrance of God and prayer, setting the lot against the remembrance and prayer reached in Surah 87.
Jonah participates in a drawing of lots and becomes one of the losers; it is a Quranic lot scene in which an assigned outcome directs a person’s next course.
The contenders cast their pens to determine who would care for Mary; this narrative allocation by cast objects provides a boundary alongside the forbidden fortune arrows.
The worshipper who asks the Lord only for this world has “no khalaq in the Hereafter”; the Quran uses the section’s measured-share noun for precisely Surah 87’s worldly choice.
Beside 2:200’s person with no afterlife share, this speaker asks the Lord for good in both worlds, showing a choice of portion that does not discard the lasting life.
Those who ask for both worlds “have a share” (نَصِيبٌ) of what they earned, completing 2:200–201’s contrast between a passing request and a valid final allotment.
Earlier peoples enjoyed their khalaq, and the present people enjoy theirs likewise before their works fail in both worlds; an allotted share can thus be consumed as passing enjoyment.
Those who purchase magic know that its buyer has no khalaq in the Hereafter; the bargain turns a chosen worldly acquisition into loss of the enduring share.
People who sell God’s covenant and their oaths for a small price have no khalaq in the Hereafter; the ayah opposes a cheap chosen return to God’s lasting portion.
God expands provision or measures it narrowly, while people rejoice in worldly life even though it is only a brief enjoyment beside the Hereafter; measure and Surah 87’s mistaken preference coincide.
Whoever wants the immediate life receives only whatever God wills and apportions, then reaches Hell; even the chosen nearer share remains under the true measurer’s will.
Whoever wants the Hereafter and strives for it faithfully has that striving thanked; this is the valid alternative to 17:18’s hastened but terminal worldly portion.
Both groups are extended gifts “from your Lord,” and His giving is not barred; the ayah identifies the real giver behind all shares before 17:21 compares their ranks.
Worldly gifts differ in rank, but the Hereafter has greater degrees and greater preference; it relocates the lottery arrow’s “highest” share into the enduring order.

Whoever seeks the harvest of the Hereafter receives increase, while the seeker of the worldly harvest receives some of it but has no afterlife share; choice becomes an apportionment with a final consequence.
The addressee must seek the afterlife home with what God has given while not forgetting his worldly share (نَصِيبَكَ); a granted portion is material for the higher choice, not its rival.
God asks whether people distribute their Lord’s mercy, then says He distributes their livelihood in worldly life; divine apportionment displaces human claims to assign the decisive share.
Passing worldly splendor is a test, whereas “your Lord’s provision is better and more lasting”; it matches the surah’s better, abiding alternative in the language of allotted sustenance.
Whatever people are given is worldly use and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting; a received share is judged by its endpoint.
Whatever people are given is merely worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for believers; the verse states the same boundary between temporary and enduring portions.
“What is with you runs out, and what is with God remains”; this gives the governing measure for the section’s worn object and its contrast between worldly and afterlife shares.
The condemned are told they used up their good things and enjoyed them in worldly life; their exhausted portion yields humiliation in the Hereafter.
Those who want worldly life and its adornment are paid their deeds there in full; the apparently complete near-world allotment is bounded by 11:16’s outcome.
For the people described in 11:15 there is nothing in the Hereafter but fire, so payment of a worldly share proves loss when the final destination is counted.
“You love the immediate” states the choice of the nearer life in the same preference structure developed from Surah 87’s apportioned lot.
“And leave the Hereafter” supplies the abandoned alternative that makes 75:20’s love a losing selection rather than mere enjoyment.
People love the immediate life and leave behind a heavy day; the object of preference and its ignored endpoint mirror the section’s two possible shares.
The transgressor “preferred the worldly life,” an almost verbal restaging of the choice in 87:16.
Hell becomes the refuge of the chooser in 79:38, showing where the apparently preferable near-world share is directed.
The alternative person fears standing before his Lord and restrains desire, supplying the opposite criterion for choosing a share.
Paradise is the refuge of the person in 79:40, completing the two apportioned destinations.
People arbitrarily assign shares of crops and cattle to God and their partners; their invented division exposes the difference between fabricated allotment and the Creator’s measure.
After 53:21 states the proposed gendered assignment, this ayah calls it an unjust division (قِسْمَةٌ ضِيزَىٰ); not every humanly declared share is a straight measure.
The prescribed fractional inheritances allocate a defined share to each relative as an obligation from God, a lawful counterpart to meat divided by gambling arrows.
The water is declared a division among the people and the she-camel, with each turn attended; measured access to water becomes an announced share rather than chance.
The she-camel has a drinking share and the people a drinking share on a known day; both portion and appointed time are fixed together.
“We shall ease him toward ease” repeats 87:8’s formula; 92:5–6 make giving, fear, and affirmation the acts that orient this directed easing.
“We shall ease him toward hardship” reverses the same formula: facilitation can direct a person toward a ruinous endpoint when his prior choice is denial and withholding.
Only “the most wretched” will enter the blazing fire, closely matching 87:11–12’s wretched person who enters the greater fire and anchoring the fire-straightening word in its Quranic moral sense.
“The most God-fearing will be kept away from it” reverses 92:15 and 87:11–12 through the same avoidance family: distance from the fire becomes salvation rather than refusal of reminder.
The person kept from fire gives wealth to purify himself, replacing the lottery’s attempt to acquire a portion with voluntary relinquishing of one.
He seeks only the face of “his Lord, the Most High” (رَبِّهِ ٱلْأَعْلَى), relocating the lot-arrow name for the highest share into the true highest object of choice.
“He will surely be satisfied” gives the giver in 92:18–20 his final granted outcome, completing the passage’s alternative economy of portion and reward.
The speaker says his Lord guided him to a straight path, the upright religion of Abraham; guidance, straightness, Lord, and the surah’s named patriarch meet in one claim.
Every earthly or bodily event is in a book before God brings it into being; prior specification parallels the hide measured before it is cut and creation planned before its finished form.
After Moses’ successive rescues and years in Midian, God says, “then you came according to a measure”; a guided life arrives at its prepared time and place.
The denier “thought and calculated” (فَكَّرَ وَقَدَّرَ), exactly the section’s planning sense of قدّر, but he applies skilled deliberation to fabricating a verdict against revelation.
The curse “how he calculated” condemns the calculation begun in 74:18, marking a moral boundary between exact planning and its corrupt use.
The repeated curse on how he calculated intensifies the boundary: the root’s craft-like intelligence does not validate the false product it prepares.
When the Lord measures a person’s provision narrowly, he says his Lord has humiliated him; the ayah exposes the human error of treating the size of a share as its worth.
The Lord expands provision for whom He wills and measures it narrowly; worldly allotments are deliberate and informed, not winnings from a random shaft.
After envying Qarun, the observers recognize that God expands and restricts provision and that Qarun’s apparent winning share was no sign of final success.
God expands provision for some servants and measures it narrowly for others; differing portions remain within His knowledge of every thing.
Expansion and measured restriction of provision are called a sign, asking the recipients to read fluctuating shares as divine ordering.
Those who reject the message cite their wealth and children, but God says the Lord expands or restricts provision; material size is not the measure of their final standing.
The Lord expands or restricts provision and replaces whatever is spent; the true apportioner can renew a share rather than merely divide a fixed carcass.
The repeated question whether they know God expands and restricts provision makes recognition of the giver, rather than possession of the portion, the ayah’s sign.
Possessor of heaven’s and earth’s keys, God expands and restricts provision; ownership of the storehouses grounds His authority to allot.
God does not spread provision without limit because people would transgress; He sends it by whatever measure He wills, making limitation part of preparation and care.
A divorce gift is due according to the affluent person’s measure and the constrained person’s measure; a human obligation is fitted to capacity rather than won by lot.
“God’s command is a measure measured” (قَدَرًا مَّقْدُورًا) presents an enacted matter as already delimited, reinforcing the dictionary sense of an assigned endpoint.
God creates humans from clay and then decrees a term, with another named term kept with Him; created life is bounded by two explicitly appointed limits.
God carries humans from weakness to strength and back to weakness and grey hair; the state-by-state arc concretizes nurture toward a determined bodily end.
After beginning the human from clay and offspring, God proportions him and gives him faculties; تسوية is one finishing stage in a larger manufacture.
God forms people and makes their forms good, provides good things, and is then identified as “your Lord”; fashioned form, provision, and lordship are one continuous care.
God creates the heavens and earth with truth and forms people well, then says the destination is to Him; good formation is directed toward an end.
The believer asks whether his companion rejects the one who created him from dust, then a drop, then proportioned him as a man; human form is a completed, staged product.
God creates the male and female pair; 53:46 identifies the single emitted drop from which this differentiated making begins.
The created pair of 53:45 comes from an emitted drop, supplying the small measured material from which distinct forms are assigned.
God is responsible for the path’s right direction while some paths deviate; this is the moral boundary between the straightened, pointed course and crooked alternatives.
Moses asks that his Lord guide him to the level or right way (سَوَآءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ), joining guidance to the section’s straight/even vocabulary.
The question “are you content with worldly life rather than the Hereafter?” treats the two lives as an explicit selection, then measures worldly enjoyment as little beside the next.

Moses describes his staff as a tool for support and herding; its lived role as a carried guide gives a concrete object to the section’s dictionary claim that a staff is called hādī because it goes before its bearer.
Iron blocks are heated until they become fire and then fused with molten copper; heat here likewise serves skilled straightening and assembly rather than only punishment.
Jonah thinks God will not “constrain” him; this probable restriction-sense of the قدر root offers a boundary case where measure is experienced as enclosure rather than fitting or allotment.
